title: US moves to stop workarounds to access advanced AI chips
excerpt: The US released an interim final rule aimed at preventing remote access to advanced AI chips that circumvent the country's export controls.
content_html:
The US is cracking down on a loophole that let China get Nvidia's best chips

By Natalie Musumeci

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

and Robert Scammell

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-16T16:02:00.963Z

It could be about to get harder for some countries to access Nvidia's advanced AI chips.

The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security released an interim final rule on Monday aimed at preventing remote access to advanced AI chips that circumvent the country's export controls.

The department said that technological advances have "made it increasingly possible to access advanced American computing capabilities remotely, including through data centers located outside countries subject to US export restrictions."

The move comes as Nvidia faces intense scrutiny over the export of its AI chips in the wake of a scandal involving a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed that led to Jensen Huang's resignation as the US chipmaker's CEO.

Megaspeed has drawn US scrutiny over allegations that it helped divert restricted Nvidia chips to Chinese customers. The company has denied any wrongdoing.

Under the Commerce Department's interim final rule, a license would be required to export advanced AI chips to firms headquartered in Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Brazil — and Singapore. These countries, the Trump administration said, "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."

Shares in Nvidia were down about 1.6% after the market opened Monday.

The Commerce Department's rule would establish new restrictions on exports, re-exports, or transfers to overseas data centers that remotely supply "significant volumes of compute" to companies headquartered in Macau or locations in the department's D:5 group, which includes China, Iran, Russia, and North Korea.

"These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using US advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models," the rule says.

As part of compliance with the new provision, data centers and chip exporters would be required to perform "robust due diligence" on their customers. The department said it would be "actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion" of the ruling.

The ruling could be another blow for Nvidia, which holds roughly 90% of the market share for AI computing.

Huang resigned last week after he admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife following a New York Times report that said he had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a former top executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer.

The report said American officials had concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset gathering information for Beijing. China has denied the allegations.

On the day of Jensen Huang's admission, Nvidia's board said it was launching an investigation into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Natalie has covered Donald Trump’s criminal and civil cases, the wave of lawsuits against the second Trump administration, the indictment and criminal trial of Sean “Diddy” Combs, the shooting death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, and the legal battles facing Elon Musk and his companies. Natalie came to Business Insider in June 2021 as a breaking news reporter, focusing on the most interesting angles on the day's trending news. Natalie largely drove BI’s coverage around the fatal “Rust” shooting involving Alec Baldwin and the disappearance and murder of Gabby Petito.Prior to joining BI, Natalie worked for the New York Post, the New York Daily News, and The Brooklyn Paper. She has an extensive background covering crime and courts. During her more than 12-year journalism career, she did a stint covering the police beat out of the New York Police Department's headquarters. Natalie, a Brooklyn native, graduated from Brooklyn College in 2012 with a degree in journalism.
